source_read: PDF, pp. 1-9 (Forensic Sci Int 378 (2026) 112699): full text read. Fig. 1 read at 300 dpi; pp. 3, 5 and 6 checked on the rendered page; Tables 1-2 read. The supplementary Table 3 (category C) was not available.

claims.overstatement: None as worded. But the brief asks for both directions where the source has both, and this source has both for THC. The fall in femoral blood between repeated post-mortem samples (one study, ref 30) sits beside a statement that THC in femoral blood after death was higher than in samples from life (refs 30, 42; p. 6). The review also reports rabbit heart-blood THC rising by 2 h after death while lung THC fell (ref 32; p. 5). Saying both ('fell between repeated samples after death, but was higher after death than in samples from life') would match the source and strengthen 'hard to read'.
claims.note: Borra et al. part only. The THC fall rests on a single cited human study (ref 30, Chu et al. 2021). No sizes, no number of cases.

anchors.extracted: Among significant post-mortem decreases in femoral blood between sampling time points: THC (one study, ref 30), with 6-MAM, risperidone, 9-OH-risperidone and caffeine. No sizes or case numbers given.

anchors.locator: 4.1.1 Early PMR, 3rd paragraph (p. 5); 5.2 AM and PM sampling, 2nd paragraph (p. 6)
anchors.extracted: Other direction: femoral THC after death was reported higher than ante-mortem concentrations (refs 30, 42). In rabbits, THC in heart blood was significantly higher 2 h after death while lung THC fell (ref 32). No sizes.

claims.overstatement: The facts check, but three paraphrases run slightly stronger than the source. (1) The heart-to-femoral ratio: the review says a ratio different from 1 suggests redistribution only if central and femoral levels were equal at death, says it is no marker of extent, and adds that a ratio of 1 does not exclude redistribution. 'Shows that change after death occurred' should read 'can indicate', and the ratio-of-1 point should be added. (2) 'Concludes that the size of the change cannot yet be tied to drug properties or to features of the case': the review says evidence linking redistribution to specific variables is often lacking. It says drug properties are 'only part of the toxicological puzzle', with general consensus that some properties contribute (e.g. basic drugs), and calls case features underexplored but promising, citing significant C/P differences by BMI, decomposition state and other variables. 'Can so far be tied only partly to drug properties, and features of the case are little studied' is closer. (3) The 17 h mean covers only studies where the interval was available or estimated (12 references, 7 of them outside Tables 1-2, including reports of one and two cases, refs 76-77). 'Does not appraise the studies' is fair: there is no study-level appraisal. Designs are ranked A/B/C by expected contribution, and Fig. 1 lists quality among reasons for excluding 17 publications, without criteria.
claims.note: Borra et al. part only. Checked: search on 18 April 2025 in PubMed (524) and Embase (448), 793 after duplicates, 87 selected (Fig. 1: category A multiple time points 29, B ante- vs post-mortem 7, C single time point 51). The 87 include animal and cadaver studies. Rises in femoral blood: 12 substances (amisulpride, chlorpromazine, clozapine, fentanyl, fluoxetine, methadone, mirtazapine, olanzapine, promethazine, quetiapine, sertraline, zuclopenthixol). Falls: 5 (6-MAM, risperidone, 9-OH-risperidone, caffeine, THC). Both lists are introduced as non-exhaustive. No sizes anywhere. Animals: heart blood morphine higher 5 min after death (rats), citalopram 15 min (rats); rabbit femoral morphine higher immediately after death. Internal inconsistency: the text says 672 excluded, but 793 - 104 = 689, matching the sum of the Fig. 1 boxes (114+104+219+19+143+90).

anchors.locator: 2. Literature search and selection strategy (both paragraphs); Fig. 1 (p. 3)
anchors.extracted: PubMed and Embase searched 18 April 2025. 793 records after duplicates; reviews, method/ex vivo, non-toxicology, formation/degradation, case series under 5, and no-peripheral-blood single-time-point studies excluded; 104 read in full, 17 more excluded (language, quality and conference abstract, per Fig. 1); 87 included, in 3 design categories (A 29, B 7, C 51). Only femoral blood counted as peripheral, femoral being considered less susceptible to change. Text says 672 excluded where the figure implies 689.

anchors.locator: 4.1.1 Early PMR, pH and lung reservoir, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Animal studies: heart-blood morphine significantly above the ante-mortem level 5 min after death (rats); femoral morphine raised immediately after death (rabbits); heart-blood citalopram raised at 15 min (rats). Lung concentrations of basic drugs fell while (cardiac) blood rose in many studies. Large between-animal variability, small groups.

Human repeated sampling: large variability between drugs and between cases of the same drug. Significant femoral-blood increases for 12 substances including fentanyl and methadone; decreases for 5 including 6-MAM and THC. No sizes. Two studies grouped rather than paired cases. Within minutes in animals, but the interval from death to first human sample, where available or estimated, averaged 17 h (range 1-292 h), so earlier change was missed.

anchors.locator: 5.2 AM and PM sampling, 1st paragraph; 5.3 C/P ratio, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Ante- vs post-mortem comparisons cannot separate redistribution from metabolism or excretion before death, incomplete absorption, or unrecorded later doses. Hospital samples are usually plasma or serum and need a blood/plasma correction. A central/peripheral ratio different from 1 hints at redistribution only if levels were equal at death; it does not give the extent, and a ratio of 1 does not exclude redistribution. Femoral blood itself changes after death.

anchors.locator: 6.1 Limitations current knowledge regarding PMR, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; 6.2 Case dependent variables
anchors.extracted: Redistribution clearly occurs, but evidence linking it to specific variables is often absent. Drug properties are only part of the picture: no clear correlation between volume of distribution or lipophilicity and the C/P ratios tabulated by Leikin et al.; ionisation of basic drugs may contribute. Case variables (trauma, resuscitation, BMI, decomposition, body position) are underexplored, with significant C/P differences reported for methadone by BMI, THC by decomposition and fentanyl by several variables.

claims.overstatement: None as worded ('found higher ... than in samples taken in life', 'relayed without sizes'). The cross-reference to change after death should not be read as showing the excess is redistribution. The review itself says increases over ante-mortem values cannot be unequivocally attributed to it (incomplete absorption when the sample was drawn, unrecorded later doses), and that hospital samples are usually plasma or serum, not whole blood.
claims.note: Borra et al. part only. MDMA (with MDA) is named among 'amphetamines' found higher in femoral blood than ante-mortem (refs 38, 82). Ref 38 (Elliott 2005) concerns fatalities following hospital admission. No sizes or case numbers.

anchors.extracted: Higher femoral-blood concentrations after death than ante-mortem were reported for amphetamines (MDMA, MDA; refs 38, 82), among other drugs. Antidepressants are reported most often. No sizes.

Caveats: rises over ante-mortem values cannot be unequivocally attributed to redistribution (absorption or distribution incomplete at sampling; unrecorded doses after). Hospital patients differ from forensic cases, ante-mortem samples are often plasma or serum, and some tubes absorb drugs.

claims.overstatement: None as worded. The 6-MAM fall rests on one cited study (ref 16, mortuary admission against autopsy blood), and no size is given. For opioids the review also reports both directions against ante-mortem samples: 6-MAM, morphine and codeine both higher and lower in post-mortem blood (ref 40), and free morphine higher after death (refs 41, 42). It notes that microbial metabolism can lower, and glucuronide hydrolysis can raise, concentrations after death.
claims.note: Borra et al. part only. Within this source the 'heroin can be missed' direction is supported by the 6-MAM decrease and by microbial degradation as a mechanism (p. 5, 4.1.2).

anchors.extracted: Significant post-mortem decrease in femoral-blood 6-monoacetylmorphine (6-MAM) between sampling time points (one study, ref 16). No size given.

anchors.locator: 4.1.2 Late PMR, 2nd paragraph (p. 5); 5.2 AM and PM sampling, 3rd paragraph (p. 6)
anchors.extracted: Microbial drug metabolism after death may lower concentrations. Opioids (6-MAM, morphine, codeine): both higher and lower post-mortem than ante-mortem (ref 40). Free morphine significantly higher after death (refs 41, 42), possibly partly from glucuronide hydrolysis.

The reference list confirms ref 76 (proof of concept, two cases) and ref 77 (one butyrfentanyl case). Refs 52 (Sawyer 1988) and 53 (Nagasawa 2016) are not in Tables 1-2.

risk_of_bias.note: I agree with the overall 'some concerns'. The 'appraisal' domain is borderline: the card's own reasoning says the included studies are not appraised and results are relayed as significant or not, which on the Leikin card was rated high. Design-level appraisal is the review's stated purpose and is done carefully (categories A-C, the AM/PM and C/P limitations, grouped analyses named), so 'some concerns' is defensible. Logged for the senior author: rating this domain high would, by rule, make the overall high.

interpretation_gap.note: I agree it is 'minor'. The points are correct: animal-derived mechanisms in the abstract, 'likely for all compounds', and absent changes explained by redistribution before the first sample.

missed: §6.2 (p. 7) also cites other groups' significant differences in C/P ratios between subgroups: methadone by BMI (ref 98), THC by state of decomposition (ref 99), fentanyl by several variables (ref 100). This bears on cl_gen_deaths_level_changes, whose 'cannot yet be tied ... to features of the case' is stronger than the review. The review calls such variables underexplored but promising, with some associations reported.

§2 (p. 2) states the general consensus that femoral blood is less susceptible to redistribution than other peripheral blood (refs 4-7). This could support the claim's 'the sample thought least open to change' alongside Ferner, together with §5.3's point that femoral blood itself changes after death.
